type=plugin source=npm:opencode-autocode created=2026-10-18T18:04:09.280Z firstSeen=2026-11-01T21:11:48.277Z published=2026-10-21T07:22:30.422Z maintainers=expiracy repoId=1421337448 stars=1 npm30d=?

Model-based shell command approval for **OpenCode 2**. AutoCode reviews pending approval requests using your coding model or a separate reviewer. - **Automatic reviews:** approve, ask you, or deny each eligible command. - **Native settings:** choose models and limits with `/autocode config`. - **Visible decisions:** inspect recent verdicts, reasons, models, and timings with `/autocode log`. - **Your restrictions apply:** resolved permission denies and OpenCode hard policies stay enforced. ![AutoCode settings popup inside the full OpenCode application](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/expiracy/autocode/3cc6181ca9e7f02c8511a71dc1a1c054272c5d91/docs/assets/settings.png) *Native settings in OpenCode 2.0.28, captured with an isolated test profile. [Capture details](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/3cc6181ca9e7f02c8511a71dc1a1c054272c5d91/docs/assets/README.md).* ## Install Add this entry to `plugins` in your global `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` or `opencode.json`, then restart OpenCode: ```jsonc { "plugins": [ { "package": "opencode-autocode@0.1.0", "options": {} } ] } ``` - OpenCode installs the package; keep **one** global AutoCode registration. - This example pins **0.1.0**. `@latest` follows the default release; `@next` follows prereleases. Check [npm versions](https://www.npmjs.com/package/opencode-autocode?activeTab=versions). - Tested with **OpenCode 2.0.28** on Linux and macOS. Requires the v2 plugin API; development uses Node.js **22.18+**. AutoCode reviews only shell requests that OpenCode resolves to **`ask`**. Existing `allow` rules skip review. If you need an `ask` rule, follow the [permission configuration guide](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/docs/configuration.md#enable-reviews): rule order matters, so preserve your existing denies. Open `/autocode config`, choose your reviewer, and save. Try: > Run exactly this shell command: `printf autocode-check`. Then report its output. An approved command runs automatically. An `ask` verdict or review failure leaves the normal approval prompt with an `autocode:` explanation. ## Commands | Command | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `/autocode config` | Enable reviews; choose model, variant, timeout, and context budget. | | `/autocode log` | Search, inspect, refresh, or clear this project's latest 100 reviews. | | `/autocode status` | View effective settings, including project overrides. | | `/autocode help` or `/autocode` | Show command help. | All four also appear in the command palette and work while automatic reviews are disabled. They make no model calls. Settings and diagnostic failures show native error notifications, with details and retry actions in the relevant dialog. ![AutoCode review popup over the OpenCode conversation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/expiracy/autocode/3cc6181ca9e7f02c8511a71dc1a1c054272c5d91/docs/assets/review-log.png) *Demonstration review using an isolated test provider. A logged verdict records the review; it does not prove command execution.* ## Defaults and boundaries | Setting | Default | | --- | --- | | Approval model | Inherit the proposing assistant's model and variant. | | Review timeout | 30 seconds. | | Context budget | 64,000 serialized JSON characters. | | Enabled | Yes. | - One tool-free model call per eligible request; provider latency and charges apply. - Reviews include the full command, working directory, and conversation. A separate provider receives that context. - Missing evidence, oversized context, invalid responses, timeouts, and provider errors fall back to manual approval. Context is never truncated to obtain approval. - Model judgments can be wrong. Set firm restrictions in OpenCode permissions and policies; each approval covers only one request. - The durable project log excludes raw command/conversation/provider-error fields. Reasons may quote context; review them before sharing. ## Guides and support - [Configuration, permission rules, models, and settings](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) - [Local installation, troubleshooting, updates, and removal](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/docs/troubleshooting.md) - [Contributing](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Release checklist](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/RELEASING.md) · [Changelog](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) - [Report an issue](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/issues) with versions and sanitized diagnostics. CI tests one recorded tarball through installation and native host integrations. Manual delivery defaults to rehearsal; npm publication requires human approval. GitHub release packages use version tags and reviewable drafts. Licensed under [MIT](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/main/LICENSE). [![Support on Ko-fi](https://ko-fi.com/img/githubbutton_sm.svg)](https://ko-fi.com/expiracy)

# Native UI captures

These screenshots show the full OpenCode terminal viewport with AutoCode's native
popup over the surrounding application. They were captured on 20 October 2026
from source commit `0ef61c1dded4258f3b4f36841e19426dc5a9c63a`, using AutoCode
`0.1.0-beta.2`, OpenCode `2.0.28`, Node.js `26.3.0`, and Python `3.14.0` on
macOS arm64.

- `settings.png` shows `/autocode config` with AutoCode's default settings. No
  settings were changed or saved.
- `review-log.png` shows the review details opened from `/autocode log`, including
  the reviewer verdict, model, reason, duration, and demonstration session ID.

The capture used a fresh disposable project, HOME, OpenCode profile, database,
configuration, cache, data, and state directories. A loopback scripted provider
returned an ALLOW verdict for an imported harmless `printf docs-check` transcript.
This exercised the real native permission hook and persisted one review entry.
Importing the transcript did not execute a process; the visible conversation
explicitly labels the tool output as a recorded fixture. Its model verdict and
45 ms duration illustrate the interface, not real-provider quality or latency.
The provider received exactly one tool-free review request. Opening the dialogs
made no additional model requests.

The OpenCode client ran in a fresh 100-column by 38-row PTY. Its actual emitted
terminal stream was decoded with pexpect `4.9.0` and pyte `0.8.2`, then every cell
of the viewport was rendered with Pillow `11.3.0`, Menlo at 18 px, and 11 by 24 px
cells. Both PNGs are 1100 by 912 px. Characters, colours, highlighting, positions,
and native text truncation come from the recorded cell buffer. Neither image was
cropped to the popup; no interface text or controls were invented, rearranged,
or retouched. The surrounding example conversation, Build/model footer, and
disposable project path are part of the actual native viewport.

No existing user profile, personal conversation, account credentials, desktop
capture, paid model, or real provider was used. The temporary client, native
server, and fixture provider were stopped after capture. The images are
provided under the repository's MIT licence.

## Logo assets

`logo-dark.svg` and `logo-light.svg` preserve the supplied AutoCode wordmark and green approval badge. `logo.svg` uses the same dark-variant paths and palette, with an accessible title, 18 px padding and a fixed dark background so the README header remains readable on both light and dark pages. No external fonts, scripts or resources are used.

# Changelog

## 0.1.0 — Unreleased

- Prepare the first stable release of AutoCode under the MIT licence, with model-based command review, native configuration, durable review logs, and OpenCode permission and hard-policy enforcement.
- Use the `latest` npm channel and version-pinned stable installation examples.
- Include controlled GitHub Actions publication, immutable source tags, verified package assets, explicit channel selection, and the GitHub asset upload fix from the unreleased candidates below.

## 0.1.0-beta.4 — Unreleased

- Correct GitHub release-asset HTTP framing by sending the exact verified byte length. A real local HTTP test exercises the installed GitHub CLI with binary and Unicode bytes.
- Prepare a fresh tagged candidate after the previous Actions run created immutable `v0.1.0-beta.3` and a partial draft before its upload failed. That tag remains unchanged; the previous candidate has not been published to npm.

## 0.1.0-beta.3 — Unreleased

- Add a manual **Publish npm package** workflow: rehearsal by default, direct OIDC publication after required human approval in the protected `npm-production` GitHub environment.
- Require the immutable version tag to identify the exact source commit, publish the CI-tested tarball without repacking or lifecycle scripts, and verify public registry integrity with provenance enabled.
- Retain the separate npm staging path. `0.1.0-beta.2` was published from its OIDC stage on 20 October 2026; this fresh version keeps that published version immutable.

## 0.1.0-beta.2 — 2026-10-20

Published to npm under `next` after human approval of the CI-tested OIDC stage.
The public archive matches the staged bytes; fresh registry installation and all
20 native checks passed on macOS with OpenCode 2.0.28. See the
[release verification record](RELEASING.md#published-beta2-verification).

- Show native error notifications for settings, log, status, and unexpected UI failures, while keeping drafts and retry controls available. Notification failures do not repeat saved changes.
- Add a manual GitHub release rehearsal and draft action, with immutable version tags and the exact CI-tested package, manifest, and checksums. Human publication remains separate.
- Shorten the README, preserve detailed configuration and troubleshooting guides, and add Ko-fi support links.

- Present the native settings and review screenshots in the npm README, with
  versioned image links and demonstration captions.
- Correct installation and release status now that the first beta is public.
- Add the AutoCode logo and show settings and review popups in the full application viewport.

## 0.1.0-beta.1 — 2026-10-18

First npm release as `opencode-autocode`, using the `next` distribution tag, with the AutoCode
plugin ID and `/autocode config` command. Tested with OpenCode 2.0.28.

- Review individual pending shell commands with the proposing model and variant,
  or a separately configured reviewer.
- Return allow, ask, or deny; retain manual approval when evidence is incomplete,
  the response is invalid, a provider fails, or the deadline expires.
- Preserve OpenCode permission denies, saved-approval precedence, and hard tool
  policies, including compound commands.
- Configure global settings in the native terminal UI, with connected model and
  variant choices, JSONC preservation, backups, and revision checks.
- Inspect the latest 100 project reviews with `/autocode log`, including reviewer
  verdicts, reasons, model choices, and timings. Refresh or clear the history in
  the native viewer; command and conversation payloads are excluded.
- Show effective project settings with `/autocode status` and command help with
  `/autocode help` or bare `/autocode`. The old `settings` alias is removed.
- Provide bounded, tool-free reviews without truncating command or conversation
  evidence.
- Distribute built JavaScript and type declarations under the MIT licence.

# Contributing to AutoCode

Use Node.js 22.18 or newer and npm. This project targets the OpenCode v2 plugin API and is tested with OpenCode 2.0.28 on Linux and macOS. CI checks Node.js 22.18 and 24; Windows host integration is not part of the verified support matrix.

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run check
npm run lint:workflows
```

`check` runs TypeScript checking, unit tests, and the production build. Keep changes focused and include a regression test for changed behavior. Permission failures must continue to require manual review or reject the request; they must never create an automatic approval.

`lint:workflows` uses a pinned actionlint 1.7.12 release with checked SHA-256
digests for Linux/macOS x64 and arm64. Its first run downloads the official
archive; later runs verify the archive cached in the system temporary directory.
It does not install a global tool or require npm development dependencies.

The release-upload HTTP regression also requires GitHub CLI (`gh`) on `PATH`.
It uses an isolated configuration, a dummy token, and a loopback server; no
GitHub sign-in or remote mutation is needed.

## Native integration test

With an OpenCode v2 binary installed:

```sh
npm run smoke
```

The smoke test packs and installs AutoCode in a temporary global configuration, starts an isolated OpenCode server, and uses a local fake provider. It checks inherited and separate reviewers, hard rejection precedence, config/log/status/help commands, model choices, settings persistence, and project-scoped review history. It also verifies that directory aliases share history and logging does not turn reviewer verdicts into execution guarantees. The fake reviewer always returns `allow`, so rejection checks test OpenCode's enforcement independently of model judgment.

This test does not send model traffic to an external provider or change your installed configuration. It uses `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` when available, otherwise `opencode` on `PATH`. To select another binary:

```sh
OPENCODE_BIN=/absolute/path/to/opencode npm run smoke
```

For release preparation, also test installation with a fresh npm cache and normal
dependency and peer resolution:

```sh
npm run smoke:registry
```

This downloads package dependencies from npm and runs the same native scenarios.
The plugin under test is installed from its local tarball, and all model traffic
still uses the local fake provider. `npm run release:check` combines local release
preparation checks; the [release workflow](RELEASING.md) separately tests one
identified archive across the full CI matrix.

To run the native suite against an already built package without repacking it:

```sh
node test/smoke.mjs --artifact artifacts/package.tgz --diagnostics-dir diagnostics/native
```

The test reads package metadata from that archive, installs it with a fresh npm
cache and lifecycle scripts disabled, and loads its installed server/TUI
entrypoints. It retains sanitized host logs and result metadata when requested.
Do not upload temporary profiles, credentials, or conversation payloads.

After publishing the manifest version, verify the actual npm package and OpenCode's
registry loader with `npm run smoke:published`. This uses fresh npm and OpenCode
caches, installs by the exact package name and version, and runs the native suite
without using this checkout's built files or your provider connections.

## Opt-in real provider validation

Keep a local OpenCode server running with this checkout registered globally, and explicitly select a connected coding model and, optionally, a separate reviewer:

```sh
npm run test:live -- --model provider/model --variant variant --reviewer provider/reviewer
```

Replace the placeholders with models available through your existing OpenCode connection and a supported variant. Omit `--reviewer` to skip the separate reviewer case. The variant defaults to `low` if omitted. Use `--server http://127.0.0.1:PORT` if your local server uses a different address from the default `http://127.0.0.1:49374`.

This check makes real model calls and incurs normal provider costs. It reads the local OpenCode service credentials and only permits loopback servers. It uses temporary conversations and project settings, executes a harmless `printf`, and evaluates destructive or adversarial examples as imported transcripts without executing those commands. It checks authorized commands, unknown scripts, unrelated and prohibited deletion, prompt injection, and a separate reviewer when requested. Reports are written under the ignored `.live-validation/` directory.

## Packaging and releases

PRs, merge queues, and pushes to `main` run typechecking, tests, workflow linting,
one package build, fresh-cache artifact installation on Node.js 22.18/24, and
native OpenCode 2.0.28 integrations on Linux/macOS. The package job records its
source commit, version, licence, release channel, and checksums; all consumers
download the same immutable artifact ID. The stable **CI required** aggregate
must pass before merging. Diagnostics are retained for 14 days and the package
for 30 days; download evidence you need to keep longer.

Run `npm pack --dry-run` to inspect local package contents; its prepack hook builds
the distributable. Use the [release checklist](RELEASING.md) for delivery. The
manual **Release** workflow defaults to rehearsal. Explicit staging from `main`
uses stage-only npm OIDC and the protected `npm-staging` environment, and a human
must approve the stage at npm with 2FA. Do not add publishing tokens or automatic
final approval. Beta releases use `next`; stable releases use `latest`.

Submit focused changes through [GitHub](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode). Include what changed and the checks you actually ran. Contributions use the project's [MIT license](LICENSE).

# Releasing AutoCode

AutoCode ships as `opencode-autocode` under the MIT licence. The package requires
Node.js 22.18 or newer and the OpenCode v2 plugin API. CI checks Node.js 22.18 and
24 and runs native integrations with OpenCode 2.0.28 on Linux and macOS. Windows
host support is not part of this release's verified scope.

`0.1.0-beta.2` is public on npm under `next`, following human approval of its
OIDC stage on 20 October 2026. Its registry archive and native installation are
verified below. The earlier `0.1.0-beta.1` first shipped on 18 October and replaced
the `0.0.0-stage` placeholder as `latest` on 20 October. Check the live registry
tags when selecting the default install version.

This checkout prepares the still-unreleased stable `0.1.0` for GitHub Actions
publication under `latest`. The earlier `v0.1.0-beta.3` tag identifies its failed draft-upload
candidate and remains unchanged. The stable candidate includes the HTTP upload fix and explicit publication channel selection.
A passing rehearsal or uploaded stage alone does not establish publication.

they do not certify future candidates or add host/platform support. Product
logos, screenshots, and the Ko-fi link were also verified in the public archive.

## Delivery contract

Pull requests, merge queues, and pushes to `main` run `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
It typechecks and tests on both supported Node versions, lints the workflows with
checksummed actionlint 1.7.12, and builds JavaScript and **one npm tarball**. Its
`artifacts/manifest.json` records the source commit, repository, package name and
version, MIT licence, release channel, filename, SHA-256, SHA-512 integrity, and
build Node/npm versions. The packaged default is `next` for prereleases and
`latest` for stable versions. Direct publication can explicitly select `latest`
for a new beta. The staging workflow keeps the packaged default; neither workflow
retags an already published version.

The uploaded package contains `package.tgz` and `manifest.json`. CI passes its
immutable GitHub artifact ID to every consumer. Fresh-cache installation checks
on Node.js 22.18 and 24 and native OpenCode checks on Linux and macOS verify and
install that exact archive, without rebuilding or repacking it. Consumer
installation disables lifecycle scripts and resolves runtime dependencies and
peers normally from npm. Native tests use temporary profiles and a local fake
provider; they do not use maintainer provider connections or execute the
rejection fixtures.

The aggregate **CI required** job passes only when workflow lint, unit checks,
packaging, installation, and native integrations all pass. Failure, cancellation,
or skipping any dependency fails the aggregate. Require this check from the
GitHub Actions app in `main` protection, require branches to be up to date, and
apply the protection to administrators. Do not add path filters that prevent the
required workflow from running. See the repository's actual protection settings
before claiming merge enforcement is active.

Actions are pinned to commit SHAs, jobs have timeouts, checkout credentials are
not persisted, and normal jobs use read-only repository permissions. Dependabot
proposes weekly npm and Actions updates. Package artifacts are retained for 30
days and diagnostics for 14 days. Host diagnostics include sanitized logs and
result metadata, not profiles, credentials, or conversation payloads. Download
release evidence before its retention period expires.

## One-time delivery setup

The workflow is ready to rehearse without npm credentials. Staging additionally
requires both external gates below; workflow source alone does not configure
them.

1. In GitHub, create the `npm-staging` environment. Allow deployments only from
   branch `main`, without a matching tag rule. The staging job names this
   environment, and npm must match the same name. A required GitHub reviewer can
   add an earlier staging gate; final npm approval remains separate.
2. As a package maintainer, configure an npm trusted publisher for package
   `opencode-autocode`, repository `expiracy/autocode`, workflow filename
   `release.yml`, and environment `npm-staging`. Allow **staging only**. Leave
   direct publishing and dist-tag modification disabled. Using an interactive
   maintainer session with 2FA, the equivalent CLI command is:

   ```sh
   npm trust github opencode-autocode \
     --repo=expiracy/autocode \
     --file=release.yml \
     --environment=npm-staging \
     --allow-stage-publish
   ```

   npm trust administration requires interactive maintainer authentication and
   account 2FA; a stored automation token is not a substitute. Check the actual
   trust entry with `npm trust list opencode-autocode` or npm's package settings.
   npm requires a new trust entry to be validated within two days. If it expires,
   recreate it when an explicitly requested staging run is ready.

The `release.yml` / `npm-staging` binding was configured, inspected as stage-only,
and used successfully for beta.2 on 20 October 2026. This does not configure the
separate production binding or change npm's legacy-token access policy.

Use GitHub-hosted runners. The staging job pins npm 12.2.0, satisfying staged
publishing's npm 11.15/Node 22.14 minimum. It has `contents: read` and
`id-token: write`; other jobs in the staging workflow do not get an OIDC token. The delivery helper rejects
missing OIDC identity and token authentication instead of falling back to a
stored npm key. Do not add `NPM_TOKEN`, `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, npm credentials, or a
direct-publish fallback to staging. Direct publication uses the separate,
explicitly requested and human-gated `publish.yml` path below.

Check npm's package publishing access settings too. Requiring 2FA and disallowing
traditional publish tokens keeps all automated delivery on the approved OIDC
path. Review existing trusted publishers so direct publishing is allowed only by the separate `publish.yml` /
`npm-production` binding, never by the staging binding. Changing these settings is a maintainer action, not
something a rehearsal verifies.

## Prepare the candidate

1. Update `package.json` and `package-lock.json` together. Use a prerelease version
   for beta delivery, update `CHANGELOG.md`, and keep README/example version pins
   aligned. Set `publishConfig.tag` to `next` for prereleases or `latest` for stable
   versions; artifact verification rejects a mismatched channel. npm versions
   cannot be reused after publication.
2. Confirm licence, exported server and TUI entrypoints, documentation, runtime
   versions, and OpenCode support. Do not include local state, credentials,
   validation transcripts, or caches in the package.
3. Merge the candidate through a pull request after **CI required** passes. Keep
   the source commit you intend to release available on protected `main`.
4. For a local check before opening the PR:

   ```sh
   npm ci --ignore-scripts
   npm run check
   npm run lint:workflows
   npm run smoke:registry
   ```

   Local smoke checks are useful preparation; they do not replace the exact
   artifact checks in the release workflow.

## Rehearse, then request staging

Open GitHub Actions → **Release** → **Run workflow**, choose `main`, and leave
`delivery` at its default `rehearsal`. The equivalent CLI request is:

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f delivery=rehearsal
```

The workflow runs the full CI pipeline at its dispatch commit. Rehearsal downloads
and verifies the tested artifact and reports its manifest, without requesting
OIDC credentials or sending anything to npm. Inspect the actual run, aggregate
result, manifest, package contents, and diagnostics. A successful run does not
prove npm trust is configured.

Only when a maintainer explicitly wants to submit that candidate for review,
select `delivery: stage` from `main`:

```sh
gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f delivery=stage
```

This run again creates one package and tests that same artifact. After every CI
check passes, the `npm-staging` job verifies the downloaded artifact's source,
version, licence, release channel, and checksums, then submits the existing
archive using npm OIDC staged delivery. It does not run project install/build
scripts, rebuild the archive, or publish it. Retain the workflow URL, source
commit, version, checksum manifest, and npm stage identifier as the review record.
A failed OIDC exchange or stage submission fails delivery; fix the configuration
instead of substituting a token.

## Prepare a GitHub draft

The separate **Prepare GitHub release** workflow (`github-release.yml`) defaults
to a rehearsal. Open GitHub Actions → **Prepare GitHub release** → **Run
workflow**, select `main`, leave `delivery` at `rehearsal`, and run it. The CLI
equivalent is:

```sh
gh workflow run github-release.yml --ref main -f delivery=rehearsal
```

This invocation runs CI once, downloads the exact tested artifact by its
immutable ID, and verifies `package.tgz` and `manifest.json` against the source
commit and checked package version. It generates `RELEASE_NOTES.md` and
`SHA256SUMS` without calling GitHub's release API. Inspect those files and the
sanitized `result.json` in the diagnostic artifact retained for 14 days. The
original package and manifest remain in the CI artifact for 30 days.

When a maintainer explicitly requests a draft, use the same workflow screen on
`main` and change `delivery` to `draft`, or run:

```sh
gh workflow run github-release.yml --ref main -f delivery=draft
```

Draft delivery requires protected `main` in `expiracy/autocode` and successful CI
in that invocation. Only the draft job has repository write permission. It
creates the candidate's `v<version>` source tag and a draft GitHub release with
the verified tarball, original manifest, and `SHA256SUMS`. An existing tag must
already identify the exact commit. A matching draft can receive missing assets;
conflicting assets or an already published release fail without replacement.

Review the draft's notes, source commit, asset checksums, and CI evidence before
publishing it manually. GitHub draft delivery does not stage or publish to npm.
Npm delivery and human 2FA approval use the separate steps above and below.

## Publish from GitHub Actions

**Publish npm package** (`publish.yml`) publishes directly after a human approves
its `npm-production` job in GitHub. It defaults to rehearsal and reuses the full
CI pipeline's single tested artifact. This path does not approve or reject npm
stages; staged versions share npm's version namespace and need their existing
npm approval path. Use a fresh version when changing delivery paths.

### Configure the production gate once

- Create GitHub environment **npm-production** with required reviewer
  **expiracy**, administrator bypass disabled, and a branch rule for **main**
  only (no tag rule). Self-review must remain available for this solo maintainer
  to approve a run they dispatched. The approval is a human action in GitHub.
- Configure a separate npm trusted publisher for `expiracy/autocode`, workflow
  **publish.yml**, environment **npm-production**, with direct publish enabled.
  Keep the existing `release.yml` binding stage-only. No npm token or environment
  secret is required; do not grant standalone dist-tag management.

```sh
npm trust github opencode-autocode \
  --repository=expiracy/autocode --file=publish.yml \
  --environment=npm-production --allow-publish
```

The production npm binding is not yet configured. Create it when a future
release is ready: npm requires its first successful publish within two days.

Review npm trust and GitHub environment settings after setup. The environment
name in YAML alone does not establish human protection. On 20 October 2026 the
GitHub production gate was configured with these reviewer, bypass, and main-only
rules; a future maintainer must recheck the live settings.

### Run the release

1. Merge the exact unused version and release notes through passing required CI.
2. Run **Prepare GitHub release** with `delivery=draft` at that source revision.
   It creates immutable `v<version>` and a reviewable draft package. Publication
   fails unless this tag resolves to the exact checked-out source commit.
3. Run **Publish npm package** with its default `delivery=rehearsal`. Choose
   `channel=package` to follow the packaged default, or **`channel=latest`** to
   make this new release the default install, including a beta. Inspect the
   source, version, selected and packaged channels, integrity, and diagnostics.
4. Run it again with `delivery=publish` and the **same channel**. All artifact
   checks run before GitHub presents **Review deployments** for `npm-production`.
5. Review the concrete artifact, then approve that deployment in GitHub. The job
   obtains an environment-bound OIDC identity and publishes the existing archive
   with provenance and lifecycle scripts disabled. It never rebuilds or repacks.

```sh
gh workflow run publish.yml --ref main -f delivery=rehearsal -f channel=latest
gh workflow run publish.yml --ref main -f delivery=publish -f channel=latest
```

Only the production job has OIDC permission. Its helper rejects an unexpected
repository, branch, unprotected source, workflow, environment, or legacy npm
credentials. A known public version must have identical integrity and still
resolve through the intended channel for a rerun to count as successful; it does
not overwrite versions or move tags to make a rerun pass. Registry errors fail
closed. A public integrity mismatch requires investigation and a new version.

The publish request does not approve its own environment deployment. A maintainer
must perform the final GitHub approval; do not bypass the gate with an API call.
After publication, run the registry verification below and inspect npm provenance.
`channel=latest` publishes the exact tested archive directly with that tag; it
does not rewrite its packaged `publishConfig.tag`, version, or manifest. The
review summary and receipt record both channels. This makes default installs
receive the selected beta and makes it the default version shown on npm. It does
not also advance `next`. Use `channel=package` for the normal version-based defaults.
An existing public version on another channel is refused rather than promoted;
that requires a separate maintainer action. No standalone npm dist-tag permission
is needed for a new publication.

## Human publication and verification

For the staged path, a package maintainer must review the stage in npm's **Staged Packages** tab,
compare it with the tested workflow artifact, and approve it with 2FA. Verify
name, version, source commit, integrity, package contents, release notes, and the
intended `next` or `latest` channel before approval. npm OIDC cannot perform this
approval. The separate direct-publication workflow publishes a fresh version
after GitHub approval instead of attempting stage approval.

After either publication path completes:

1. Verify registry metadata and integrity for that exact version and inspect
   `npm dist-tag ls opencode-autocode`. Confirm the selected publication channel
   resolves to this exact version; betas use `next` by default or `latest` when
   explicitly selected.
2. Run `npm run smoke:published` from the matching source revision. This installs
   the manifest version from npm with fresh caches, configures OpenCode by the
   exact package name/version, and runs the native suite. It cannot fall back to
   the local build or the tested prepublication archive.
3. Only after actual registry installation succeeds, mark the published-package
   scenario complete and update release status in the changelog. Review the matching
   GitHub draft and its existing source tag, add links to npm and the tested
   workflow run, and publish the draft manually. Do not create a second tag or
   replace a tag created by the draft workflow.

Restart the terminal client after upgrading its TUI companion. If registry
verification fails, investigate and prepare a corrected version; do not claim a
successful release check or reuse a published version.

References: [npm staged publishing](https://docs.npmjs.com/staged-publishing/),
[npm trusted publishing](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers/),
[trust configuration CLI](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-trust/),
[GitHub required checks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/troubleshooting-required-status-checks),
and [OpenCode package plugins](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/#publish).

# Configuration and command reviews

[README](../README.md) · [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md)

## Enable reviews

AutoCode only reviews the `shell` requests OpenCode resolves to `ask`. If your current rules already ask for shell approval, keep them. To make other shell requests eligible, merge an `ask` rule into your existing `permissions` array:

```jsonc
"permissions": [
  { "action": "shell", "resource": "*", "effect": "ask" }
  // Keep your more specific allow/deny rules after this broad rule.
]
```

**Preserve your existing restrictions.** OpenCode uses the last matching permission rule, so appending a broad `ask` rule after a specific `deny` can change OpenCode's resolved decision. See [permission rules](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions/) and the [complete configuration example](../examples/opencode.jsonc).

Restart OpenCode, enter `/autocode config`, and choose **Save settings** after any changes. You can also open **AutoCode config** from the command palette. The dialog lets you enable reviews, choose an approval model and its variant, adjust the timeout and context budget, and view the review log.

Try this harmless prompt in a new conversation:

> Run exactly this shell command: `printf autocode-check`. Then report its output.

With a working reviewer, the command should run automatically if the model approves it. A model can still ask for manual review; the permission prompt includes an `autocode:` explanation when AutoCode handles the request.

## Commands and review log

| Command | Opens |
| --- | --- |
| `/autocode config` | The global settings editor. |
| `/autocode log` | Recent AutoCode reviews for the current project. |
| `/autocode status` | The effective project settings, including overrides. |
| `/autocode help` or `/autocode` | Command help. |

These commands also appear in the command palette and remain available while
automatic approval is disabled. `/autocode settings` is no longer an alias;
use `/autocode config` to edit settings. None of these commands calls a model.

The review log keeps the latest **100** reviews in OpenCode's durable plugin
storage, scoped to the current project location. It survives restarts and settings
reloads. Search verdicts, reasons, models, or sessions; select an entry for its
timestamp, reviewer model and variant, duration, reason, and session ID. **Refresh**
loads newer entries, and **Clear review log** removes this project's history after
confirmation. The settings editor also has a **View review log** action.

![AutoCode review details popup with the OpenCode conversation visible behind it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/expiracy/autocode/3cc6181ca9e7f02c8511a71dc1a1c054272c5d91/docs/assets/review-log.png)

*Demonstration review in OpenCode 2.0.28 using an isolated test provider. [Capture details](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/blob/3cc6181ca9e7f02c8511a71dc1a1c054272c5d91/docs/assets/README.md).*

Entries record AutoCode's reviewer verdict or manual fallback. They do not prove
that a command ran: OpenCode can still reject a reviewer-approved command through
a hard policy. Requests already allowed or denied by OpenCode, non-shell requests,
and requests made while AutoCode is disabled do not create review entries. The
log starts recording after this version is loaded; it does not import old history.

The log has no raw command, conversation, or provider-error payload fields.
Reasons are limited to 1000 characters and may quote supplied context, so
review them before sharing diagnostics. Logging failures do not delay or change
permission decisions.

## How approval works

For each eligible request, AutoCode obtains the full originating shell command, working directory, and conversation context from OpenCode. It asks the reviewer to return one decision:

| Decision | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `allow` | Approve this pending request. |
| `ask` | Leave OpenCode's normal approval prompt for you. |
| `deny` | Reject this pending request. |

Each review applies to one request. AutoCode never saves an “Allow always” rule. Existing `allow` decisions skip review. Non-shell permissions follow OpenCode's normal behavior.

### Hard rejections stay enforced

Commands whose resolved OpenCode permission is `deny` stay blocked without calling the reviewer. This also covers compound commands containing a denied resource and conflicts with a saved “Allow always” approval. AutoCode leaves a denial from an earlier permission hook unchanged.

OpenCode's hard [tool policies](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/policies/) also remain enforced. A policy can reject a command after the reviewer returns `allow`, so a model call may occur before a policy rejection. These guarantees follow OpenCode's normal configuration precedence; AutoCode does not maintain a separate deny list or change permission rules and policies. See the [native permission hook](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/#permissions).

### Manual review on missing evidence or failure

AutoCode leaves the normal approval prompt when it lacks user intent or the full command, cannot resolve a model, receives an invalid reviewer response, encounters a provider error, or exceeds the deadline. It never approves from parsed permission resources alone: those resources can omit parts of a compound shell command.

All serialized review data must fit `maxContextChars`. AutoCode does not truncate the conversation or command to obtain approval. If the budget is exceeded, compact the session or increase the budget. Compaction may remove evidence of authorization, so the reviewer may still ask.

Model judgments can be wrong. Express firm restrictions with OpenCode permission rules or policies.

## Choose a reviewer

Omit `options.model`, or set it to `"inherit"`, to use the model and variant of the assistant that proposed the command. If that metadata is unavailable, AutoCode falls back to the session model, then OpenCode's default model.

Use **AutoCode config → Approval model** to select another connected model. This does not change the coding model. For JSON configuration, replace the registration's `options` with:

```json
{
  "model": "provider/model"
}
```

The first slash separates the provider ID from the model ID. For example, `"openrouter/vendor/model"` selects provider `openrouter` and model `vendor/model`. To choose a reasoning variant, use the object form:

```json
{
  "model": {
    "providerID": "provider",
    "id": "model",
    "variant": "high"
  }
}
```

Replace these placeholders with a connected, enabled model. `variant` is optional and must be supported by that model; the settings dialog lists available variants.

### Cost and context privacy

AutoCode uses OpenCode's existing provider connections. Each eligible request makes at most one tool-free review call, with the provider's normal latency, limits, and charges. The review includes the command, working directory, and session conversation returned by OpenCode. Choosing another provider sends that context to the selected provider. Review this choice before using AutoCode with sensitive conversations.

## Settings reference

| Option | Default | Accepted values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | Boolean. `false` leaves approvals to OpenCode. |
| `model` | Inherit | Omit, use `"inherit"`, use `"provider/model"`, or use `{ "providerID": "…", "id": "…", "variant": "…" }` with optional `variant`. |
| `timeoutMs` | `30000` | Integer from `1` to `300000`; deadline for the complete review, in milliseconds. |
| `maxContextChars` | `64000` | Integer from `1000` to `1000000`; maximum serialized review data size, in JSON characters. |

Unknown options, misspelled model fields, empty identifiers, and invalid values fail plugin setup with a configuration error.

The settings dialog edits the existing plugin `options` in your **global** OpenCode configuration. Saving preserves unrelated configuration and comments, and creates a backup under `.autocode/settings-backups/` beside that file. Concurrent edits are detected; reopen settings if the file changed while you were editing. Symlinked profiles must be edited at the original file.

OpenCode reloads saved options for subsequent reviews. Project-specific plugin options still override global defaults, so a global change may not change behavior in a project with an override. Options also remain editable directly as JSON. Closing an edited settings draft offers to discard it or keep editing.

# Installation and troubleshooting

[README](../README.md) · [Configuration](configuration.md)

## Use a local checkout

For local development or to try a specific source revision, build with **Node.js 22.18 or newer** and npm:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/expiracy/autocode.git
cd autocode
npm ci
npm run build
```

Use the [global plugin registration from the README](../README.md#install), but replace `package` with the absolute path to your checkout:

```json
{
  "package": "/absolute/path/autocode",
  "options": {}
}
```

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| `/autocode config` or the palette entry is missing | Use OpenCode v2, confirm the global plugin registration loaded, and restart OpenCode including the terminal client. For a local checkout, run `npm ci` and `npm run build` first. |
| Commands run without a reviewer | Check that AutoCode is enabled and that OpenCode resolves the request to `ask`. Existing `allow` rules skip AutoCode. |
| Commands remain blocked | Check permission denies and hard tool policies. AutoCode cannot override them. A reviewer may also deliberately return `deny`. |
| The normal prompt remains | Read its `autocode:` explanation. Check the selected provider connection, model and variant, timeout, context budget, and availability of the full command and user context. |
| The OpenCode free model rejects a review | Some free models reject isolated review requests even when they work as the coding model. Choose a separate connected reviewer in **Approval model**; keep your coding model selected. |
| Saving says multiple registrations exist | Keep one global AutoCode registration, including across `opencode.json` and `opencode.jsonc`. Remove an old local-path registration when switching to the npm package. |
| Saved settings seem ineffective in one project | Check that project's plugin options for an override. Confirm you are editing the config directory used by the running OpenCode instance. |
| The log is empty | Only reviews made by this AutoCode version appear. Existing allow/deny decisions and requests while disabled skip review. Use **Refresh** after a new review and check that you are in the same project. |
| A log entry says `allow`, but the command was blocked | The entry is AutoCode's verdict. OpenCode's hard policies can reject the command afterward. |

If the problem persists, [open an issue](https://github.com/expiracy/autocode/issues) with your OpenCode and AutoCode versions, installation method, sanitized plugin options, and the relevant error. Remove credentials and private conversation content before sharing.

Settings, log, and status failures also show a native error notification in the terminal. Keep the dialog open to review details or retry; a review-provider failure still falls back to manual approval.

## Update or uninstall

The npm example pins `opencode-autocode@0.1.0`. Use `opencode-autocode@latest` to follow the default release or pin another published version explicitly. Review the [changelog](../CHANGELOG.md) before upgrading, and restart OpenCode after changing its registration. While using a local checkout, pull the desired revision, run `npm ci` and `npm run build`, then restart OpenCode.

To pause automatic reviews, disable AutoCode in settings. To uninstall, clear any review history you want removed through `/autocode log`, remove its entry from the global `plugins` array and any project registrations, then restart OpenCode. Keep your permission rules and policies as needed for normal OpenCode approvals. Optional settings backups and OpenCode's plugin storage remain after removing a registration.
